idiom_name: abstract Authenticator interface + concrete mechanism implementations + registry/chain
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: declare one operation that maps a credential to a principal or to a failure, implement it once per mechanism, and register implementations under scheme names in a factory or configuration so the request path resolves a name instead of branching. Keep the output normalized to a single principal type; mechanisms carrying richer evidence (certificate chains, token scopes) attach it as optional detail the caller may ignore. Treat invalid credentials and verifier unavailability distinctly but deny access for both, and make chain semantics (first match, required, sufficient, optional) explicit. Where the platform already provides the seam (PAM, JAAS, ASP.NET Core authentication schemes, Django authentication backends), use it instead of rebuilding.
pitfalls: Returning a mechanism-specific principal or claims object -> callers branch on credential format and the seam disappears -> return one Principal type and expose mechanism evidence only as optional detail.

Treating provider unavailability as invalid credentials -> outages look like wrong passwords and trigger misleading lockouts -> return distinct verifier-unavailable and invalid-credential results, while denying access for both.

Registering overlapping authenticators or silently falling through a failed verifier -> an attacker selects the weakest scheme or becomes anonymous -> bind each credential shape to one verifier and make required/sufficient/optional chain semantics explicit.

Implementing retries, lockout, comparison, audit or failure mapping at every call site -> policy drifts and one endpoint becomes the bypass -> centralize those controls inside the authenticator boundary.

Storing passwords in plaintext, with a fast hash, or reversibly -> a database breach enables offline guessing or credential recovery -> use a framework KDF with a unique salt, preferably Argon2id, and rehash as parameters age.

Accepting a delegated OAuth callback without exact redirect/state/PKCE checks -> an injected code or mix-up binds the session to an attacker-controlled identity -> use Authorization Code + PKCE, validate state or nonce and issuer, then exchange the code server-side.

Relying on password verification alone against automated reuse -> credential stuffing continues across distributed sources and overwhelms the login path -> add MFA or step-up plus layered rate limits, abuse metrics and breached-password checks.

Trusting identity-carrying headers (X-Remote-User style) from any client -> anyone can forge a principal by setting the header -> accept header-based identity only from callers that first prove themselves with a validated client certificate, as the Kubernetes request-header authenticator requires.

Treating an absent/null authentication result as merely falsy at the trust check -> trust-resolver flaws like Spring Security CVE-2024-22234 let isFullyAuthenticated(null) report success -> deny explicitly on null, anonymous and remembered identities unless each tier is deliberately granted, and centralize that triage in one resolver.

Sharing one provider chain that includes anonymous or remember-me providers across every channel -> a client on an insecure transport (e.g. raw RMI) can forge an AnonymousAuthenticationToken and pass the chain -> build a per-channel authenticator set and omit anonymous/remember-me providers where they are not intended.
